previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia and tracheostomy was admitted for cough with green, blood-tinged sputum, throat pain, and inability to tolerate oral intake for two days. She had no fever, stable vital signs, and normal white blood cell count. Imaging showed no acute cardiopulmonary abnormalities, and ENT evaluation found no tracheal inflammation. A swallow study confirmed mild oropharyngeal dysphagia without aspiration, consistent with prior findings. She was managed symptomatically with pain control, dietary modifications, and continuation of home medications. She improved, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with instructions for soft diet, oral care, and follow-up with ENT and primary care.

___ is a ___ year-old female with a PMH of 
tracheobronchomalacia secondary to premature birth at 26wks, s/p 
4 airway reconstructions and tracheostomy since infancy, h/o 
chronic bronchitits and tracheitis, h/o chronic pain on 
narcotics contract presents with dyspnea and green sputum 
production x1 week concerning for recurrent tracheitis 

Patient was observed for 1 night and was non-toxic, afebrile, no 
leukocytosis, and did not demonstrate a high suction requirement 
for secretions. Her pain was well controlled with her oral home 
regimen. Tracheoscopy by ENT revealed no signs of inflammation 
with visualization to the carina, no breakdown of posterior back 
wall of trach, and no mucopurulence in airway. 

In light of this evidence, our team felt comfortable holding 
antibiotics given very low concern of bacterial 
tracheobronchitis. We elected to treat symptomatically for an 
acute upper respiratory infection. She was discharged to home 
with knowledge of ""red flag"" symptoms to return to care. 

All other home medications were continued and the patient was 
discharged without any changes to her home medications. She has 
ENT follow up scheduled.

Dear Ms. ___,

and there was more pain in your throat than usual.

(""tracheitis"").

Our ENT doctors looked in your throat and did not see any signs 
of infection.  You also did not have any fevers or signs of 
infection on your lab work.

(possibly from a virus like the common cold) that does not 
require antibiotics.  You should expect to get better naturally
